ut_chuckawalla_wall.blurb: A compact bolted wall of red sandstone on the north edge of St. George, built almost entirely of single-pitch sport lines. Expect a mix of crimps, slopers and pockets, some of them worn slick by heavy use. Most of the lines sit in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with a small handful of 5.9s and a couple of 5.13s at the top end. The wall catches sun for most of a winter day, which makes it a cold-season favorite, and it tends to be busy on weekends. The sandstone turns soft when wet, so give it a good drying-out after any rain.
ut_chuckawalla_wall.parking_note: From downtown St. George, head north on Bluff Street, passing the Sunset Boulevard intersection and continuing about a mile. A pullout sits on your left, with restrooms nearby; the wall is a very short stroll from there.
ut_chuckawalla_wall.approach: A flat, two-minute walk from the lot along a dirt track to the base of the wall.

ut_altered_states_gully.blurb: A steep-sided gully on the Grit Mill side of Little Cottonwood Canyon, holding mostly traditional lines with a few bolted ones. The climbing leans toward slabs and moderate cracks, and the stone ranges from excellent to dirty and in need of cleaning. Most routes fall between 5.9 and 5.11, with a few easier and a few harder. Easier lines can be thinly protected, so this is a place for climbers comfortable on slab and with placing their own gear. Reaching the gully involves a rough bushwhack and some trail-finding.
ut_altered_states_gully.approach: Leave the road near the Archives access road, then thrash up a faint side gully through brush and loose ground, following scraps of trail until you reach the main gully. Expect it to be awkward and slow.

ut_south_face.blurb: One of the two faces of Black Peeler Buttress, high on the south side of Little Cottonwood Canyon. Slabs and cracks dominate, with mostly traditional routes, a handful of bolted lines, a couple of aid climbs and a single boulder problem. Grades are spread widely, with the most lines around 5.8 and 5.10. The coarse-grained stone gives good friction but is often flaky because few people climb here, and many routes need two ropes to rappel. Facing south, it bakes in summer, while spring and fall are the better seasons.
ut_south_face.approach: Start from the roadside trail a short way beyond the Gate Buttress parking. Follow the dirt path beside the boulder field, then scramble up a rocky drainage to the base of the cliff, and fork left for the South Face.

ut_dairy_canyon.blurb: A high, sandstone bouldering zone at the top of the Right Fork in Joe's Valley. The rock is a bulging, pocketed hillside that reads more like a cliff band than a scatter of boulders, and the landings are good and the views open. Problems run from easy to V10, with the largest cluster in the V4 to V8 range. Sitting higher than the valley floor, it runs noticeably cooler than the Left Fork and picks up afternoon shade, which helps in warm weather. Sandstone weakens when damp, so wait several days after precipitation.
ut_dairy_canyon.parking_note: Follow the Right Fork road up past the old Trail Mountain Mine, where the pavement gives way to dirt. A short distance beyond a camp on the left, turn onto a side track and pull into the open clearing.
ut_dairy_canyon.approach: A trail climbs the hillside directly from the clearing to the boulders.

ut_great_white_icicle_area.blurb: The south side of Little Cottonwood Canyon is best known for the Great White Icicle, a four-pitch WI3 ice flow that draws more ice climbers than anything else near Salt Lake City, so expect a queue whenever it is formed. Ice season generally runs from mid-December into late February. Around it sit mostly slabby rock routes, mainly trad with some sport and a few mixed lines, mostly 5.9 to 5.11. The trail in was wiped out by avalanche debris, so expect a rough scramble over downed trees and boulders on the way to the base.
ut_great_white_icicle_area.approach: Cross the creek by the best route available for the water level, then pick through avalanche debris and fallen trees toward the climber's right side of the main falls. Parking is tight, so carpooling helps.

ut_division_wall.blurb: A popular limestone sport wall in American Fork Canyon, tucked right behind the sites of Little Mill Campground. Nearly everything is bolted, with the bulk of the lines in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, a few warm-ups around 5.9 and 5.10, and a handful of low 5.13s nearby. The canyon is known for steep, pocketed limestone, and the edges here have cleaned up with traffic though some still break off. With almost no approach, it is easy to hop on, and it fills up fast on weekends.
ut_division_wall.approach: Essentially none: the base of the wall is just behind the campsites in Little Mill Campground.

ut_watchtower_main.blurb: The main section of the Watchtower, the largest and most visited crag in Ferguson Canyon, and the first wall you meet on the hike in. It is a long, steep face scored by horizontal seams, with mostly traditional routes and a few good bolted ones. Grades center on 5.10 and 5.11, with some easier and a couple harder. Most lines have anchors suited to a single-rope rappel, and a steep walk-off exists at the west end. The wall drops into the stream, so you may need to hop rocks when the water is high. The canyon is treed and a popular summer escape.
ut_watchtower_main.parking_note: Leave your car along the right side of Timberline Drive, close to the trailhead sign at the top of the neighborhood.
ut_watchtower_main.approach: From the trailhead, follow a dirt road to a white water tank, then drop into the canyon and follow the trail up its south side to the wall.

ut_south_fork.blurb: The busiest climbing spot in Kolob Canyons, on a varnished, pocketed sandstone wall near the head of the South Fork of Taylor Creek. Short one-pitch lines, including bolted ones, share the cliff with longer free and aid routes. Trad and sport are about evenly matched, and most grades fall between 5.10 and 5.11, with a few easier and harder. Reaching it means a mellow hike of roughly 40 minutes up a braided, unofficial trail with no water. The sandstone is fragile when wet, so stay off it when the ground is damp.
ut_south_fork.parking_note: Use the obvious lot a few miles up the scenic drive in Kolob Canyons, where the road swings to the right; the trailhead is across the pavement.
ut_south_fork.approach: Cross the road and follow the braided social trail up the canyon, staying on the best-worn track. After the trail climbs onto a flat sandy floor lined with conifers, the wall appears shortly before the falls at the canyon head.
